bibliography.abstract: On 1 January 1996, Germany transferred responsibility for regional passenger rail services from the federal government to the states. Three decades later, passenger-kilometres have doubled and competitive tendering has lowered operating costs substantially, making regionalisation the most successful element of the German rail reform. Its organisational model, however, has reached the end of its life cycle: tenders now attract on average only 1.3 bids, 26 contracting authorities and some 60 transport associations maintain overlapping structures, rolling-stock procurement has repeatedly shifted risk onto passengers, and since the Court of Justice of the European Union struck down the German track-access charge cap in 2026, funding no longer covers the ordered service volume. This article reviews the motives and results of regionalisation, identifies three structural design flaws, and argues for a second reform: consolidating authorities, standardising rolling stock, deciding between a repaired market model and integrated public operation, and indexing funding to real infrastructure cost development. The submission contains an English translation followed by the German original.
bibliography.comment: English translation followed by the German original (Erfolgsmodell am Lebenszyklusende: 30 Jahre Regionalisierung des Schienenpersonennahverkehrs). 15 pages, 6 figures. Extended version with full reference list of an article published in abridged form in BAHN-REPORT 5/2026. English translation prepared with AI assistance and reviewed by the author
bibliography.title: A Success Model at the End of Its Life Cycle: 30 Years of Regionalised Regional Rail in Germany

en.what: This review evaluates the 30-year outcome of Germany decentralising regional passenger rail to its states in 1996, a policy that doubled passenger-kilometres while reducing operating costs through competitive bidding. It identifies key structural points of failure in the current system, including a drop in competition to just 1.3 bids per tender, administrative fragmentation across 26 contracting authorities and 60 transport associations, and funding shortfalls following a 2026 court ruling that overturned track-access charge caps.
en.why: It demonstrates that a long-standing market-based rail governance model has exhausted its effectiveness, offering concrete policy directions for consolidating authorities, standardising rolling stock, and indexing funding to actual infrastructure costs.
